items.title: 4.1 Graphical User Interface (GUI) Development with Tkinter

source_refs.note: Chapter opening and 4.1 (PDF 49-56) with the Tidbit, Class Activities and code listings checked against the page images; Figs 4.1 and 4.2 redrawn, plus frames and login figures. Warnings and check questions are added. Short Q1-8 and Long Q1-7 are answered here.

blocks.text: This chapter teaches how to build user-friendly Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs) with Tkinter, Python's built-in GUI toolkit: windows, frames, labels, buttons and entry fields, layouts with pack(), grid() and place(), and event handling that links user actions to functions, ending with a simple login form. It then introduces databases, SQL, connecting Python to a database, and the basic CRUD operations with SQLite or MySQL.
What is a GUI, and why is it important?

blocks.title: Graphical User Interface (GUI)
blocks.text: A GUI is a visual interface that lets users interact with software through elements such as windows, buttons, labels, menus, text boxes and forms.

GUIs make programs easier to understand and use than command-line interfaces, especially for non-technical users. They improve usability by giving visual feedback and removing the need to remember complex commands. GUI applications are used in desktop software, web applications and mobile apps (Fig 4.1).
Tkinter: Python's built-in GUI toolkit

Tkinter is Python's standard GUI toolkit and comes pre-installed with the language. It provides classes and functions for windows, buttons, labels, entry fields and other widgets. It is easy to learn and lightweight, supports event-driven programming (actions are triggered by user events), and suits small to medium GUI applications.

blocks.title: Example: a simple GUI (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
import tkinter as tk

# Create main window
window = tk.Tk()
window.title("Simple GUI Example")
window.geometry("300x200")

# Function to handle the button click (event)
def on_click():
....print("Button Clicked!")

label = tk.Label(window, text="Welcome to Tkinter")
label.pack(pady=10)

entry = tk.Entry(window)
entry.pack(pady=10)

button = tk.Button(window, text="Click Me", command=on_click)
button.pack(pady=10)

# Run the application
window.mainloop()

items: tk.Tk() creates the main window; title() and geometry() set its title and size (300 by 200 pixels).
Label displays text; Entry takes user input; Button performs an action.
command=on_click is event handling: clicking the button calls on_click(), which prints 'Button Clicked!'.
mainloop() runs the GUI and keeps the window open, waiting for events.

blocks.alt: A window titled Simple GUI Example contains the text Welcome to Tkinter, an empty entry box and a Click Me button. Arrows label them Label (shows text), Entry (takes typed input) and Button (runs a function when clicked); window = tk.Tk() marks the main window. A dashed arrow from the button leads to a note: command=on_click, a click runs on_click() and prints Button Clicked!. A footer says window.mainloop() keeps the window open and waiting for events.
blocks.caption: A simple Tkinter window and its widgets (original diagram after Fig 4.1).
blocks.long_description: Every Tkinter program has the same skeleton: create the window, create widgets inside it, place them with a layout method, link events to functions, then call mainloop().

blocks.text: Tkinter components and widgets

Tkinter's components, called widgets, are the visual elements of an application: windows, frames, buttons, text fields and more. Widgets let users enter data, choose options or perform actions; each has its own purpose, and combining them builds a complete interface. Tkinter also manages layout, so widgets can be arranged neatly.

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Create a main window and divide it into two frames. Add different widgets to each frame to organise the layout.
Creating windows and adding frames

A Tkinter program begins with a main window, the base for every other element; it can be resized, given a title and filled with widgets. Frames are sections inside the window that group related widgets, which keeps the interface clear and well arranged.

blocks.title: Example: two frames (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
import tkinter as tk

window = tk.Tk()
window.title("Tkinter Frames Example")
window.geometry("400x300")

top_frame = tk.Frame(window, bg="lightblue", height=100)
top_frame.pack(fill="x")

bottom_frame = tk.Frame(window, bg="lightgreen", height=200)
bottom_frame.pack(fill="both", expand=True)

tk.Label(top_frame, text="Top Frame", bg="lightblue").pack(pady=20)
tk.Label(bottom_frame, text="Bottom Frame", bg="lightgreen").pack(pady=20)

window.mainloop()

blocks.alt: A window titled Tkinter Frames Example is split into a light-blue top frame holding the text Top Frame and a larger light-green bottom frame holding the text Bottom Frame. Side notes: top_frame is light blue with height 100; bottom_frame is light green with fill both and expand True; each frame holds its own widgets.
blocks.caption: Frames dividing a window into sections (original diagram after the frames example).
blocks.long_description: fill='both' with expand=True lets the bottom frame grow to fill the space left when the window is resized.

blocks.text: Layout management

Layout management arranges widgets inside a window, deciding the position and size of each. Good layout makes the interface clear, easy to use and organised. Tkinter has three layout methods, each placing widgets in its own way (Fig 4.2).

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Proper layout management makes applications look neat and work well on different screen sizes.

items: pack(): places widgets one after another, vertically or horizontally. It is simple and good for small applications.
grid(): arranges widgets in rows and columns like a table. It suits forms and structured layouts; columnspan lets one widget stretch across columns.
place(): positions widgets at exact x and y coordinates. It gives the most control but needs careful adjustment.

blocks.title: Example: pack() (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
button1 = tk.Button(window, text="Button 1", width=12)
button2 = tk.Button(window, text="Button 2", width=12)
button3 = tk.Button(window, text="Button 3", width=12)
button1.pack(pady=10)
button2.pack(pady=10)
button3.pack(pady=10)

blocks.title: Example: grid() (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
button1.grid(row=0, column=0, padx=10, pady=20)
button2.grid(row=0, column=1, padx=10, pady=20)
# Button 3 spans two columns
button3.grid(row=1, column=0, columnspan=2, padx=10, pady=10)
# Keep content centred
window.grid_columnconfigure(0, weight=1)
window.grid_columnconfigure(1, weight=1)

blocks.title: Example: place() (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
button1.place(x=30, y=40)
button2.place(x=170, y=85)
button3.place(x=30, y=140)

Each example starts like the frames example (import tkinter, create a 300 by 220 window with a title, create three buttons) and ends with window.mainloop(). Do not mix pack() and grid() for widgets inside the same container: Tkinter cannot satisfy both and the program may freeze.

blocks.alt: Three small windows. pack(): Button 1, 2 and 3 stacked top to bottom. grid(): Button 1 and Button 2 side by side in row 0, and a wide Button 3 spanning both columns in row 1, with dashed grid lines. place(): Button 1 at x=30, y=40, Button 2 at x=170, y=85 and Button 3 at x=30, y=140. Notes: pack stacks in order; grid uses rows and columns and columnspan; place uses exact positions.
blocks.caption: The three layout managers (original diagram after Fig 4.2).
blocks.long_description: pack and grid adjust positions for you; place does not, so place-based windows may look wrong if the window or font size changes.

blocks.text: Designing clean and responsive interfaces

A clean interface has well-arranged widgets with enough space between them, and clear, readable text and buttons. A responsive interface adjusts its layout when the window size changes, so the program works on different screens. Proper alignment and a simple design make the interface user-friendly.
Event handling and interactivity

Event handling lets a program respond to user actions. An event is an action such as clicking a button or typing text. The program waits for events instead of running all the time; when an event occurs, a specific task is performed.

In event-driven programming the program stays idle until an event, such as a button click or key press, occurs. Each event is linked to a function that runs only when the event happens, which saves system resources; this approach is widely used in GUIs. User input comes through widgets such as entry fields and buttons; widgets are connected to functions, and when a widget is used, its function runs and processes the input.
Example: a simple login form

blocks.title: Example: login form (Python code; each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
import tkinter as tk
from tkinter import messagebox

window = tk.Tk()
window.title("Login Form")
window.geometry("300x200")

def check_login():
....username = entry_user.get()
....password = entry_pass.get()
....if username == "admin" and password == "1234":
........messagebox.showinfo("Success", "Login Successful!")
....else:
........messagebox.showerror("Error", "Invalid Username or Password")

tk.Label(window, text="Username").pack()
entry_user = tk.Entry(window)
entry_user.pack()

tk.Label(window, text="Password").pack()
entry_pass = tk.Entry(window, show="*")
entry_pass.pack()

tk.Button(window, text="Login", command=check_login).pack(pady=10)

window.mainloop()

items: Entry widgets take the username and password; show='*' hides the password as it is typed.
The Login button submits the data: command=check_login runs the check when it is clicked.
check_login() reads the input with get() and messagebox shows success or an error.
The whole program works by event-driven programming.

blocks.title: Never keep real passwords in code
blocks.text: Writing 'admin' and '1234' in the program is fine for learning, but real applications must never store passwords in the code. They keep a secure hash of each password, usually in a database, and compare hashes.

blocks.alt: Left: an event loop of four boxes joined by curved arrows: mainloop() waits, event: Login clicked, check_login() runs, message shown, and back to waiting. Right: a Login Form window with a Username entry containing admin, a Password entry showing four stars, a Login button and a green box saying Login Successful!. A note: entry.get() reads what was typed, show='*' hides the password, and the button's command= links the click to check_login().
blocks.caption: The event loop and a login form (original diagram after the login example).
blocks.long_description: The program does nothing until the user clicks Login; then the linked function runs once and the loop goes back to waiting.

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Explain event-driven ideas, then add a button that updates a label's text when it is clicked.

blocks.prompt: A button is created with command=greet() instead of command=greet. What goes wrong?
blocks.explanation: With brackets, greet() is called once while the button is being created, and its return value (usually None) is stored as the command, so clicking does nothing. command= must be given the function itself, without brackets.

blocks.prompt: Which layout method would you use for a form with labels in one column and entry fields in the next? Why?
blocks.explanation: grid(), because it places widgets in rows and columns, so each label and its entry line up in the same row.

blocks.text: Quick recap

items: GUI: visual interface; Tkinter: Python's built-in toolkit (Tk(), widgets, mainloop()).
Widgets: Label, Button, Entry, Menu, Listbox; frames group widgets.
Layouts: pack (in order), grid (rows and columns), place (exact x, y).
Event-driven: command= links a widget to a function that runs on the event.
